title: The Jaenisch Gambit
description: A variation against White playing the Spanish or Ruy Lopez. We strike at the center and immediately seize the initiative. Very fun positions leading to super complicated games. Could be a little dangerous for beginners, but try it out!

N1b4r/pp2k1pp/2np4/1B2p3/7P/4q3/PPP3P1/R.text: And we have perpetual checks via Qe3+ and Qf4+. White cannot step onto the f-file because we then bring our rook to f8 and win the game.

r1b1k2r/ppN3pp/2np4/1B2p3/7P/6q1/PPP3P1/.text: It seems we have allowed a fork, but we just move our king to defend the d6-pawn, and...

r1b1k2r/ppp3pp/2np4/1B1Np1q1/7P/8/PPP3P1.text:
White attacks our queen, and makes room for their king. The immediate Nc7+ would have ended  up losing to a future Qe3+ and Rf8+.

We'll play our queen to g3, where we threaten a perpetual check if White moves the knight.

r1b1qrk1/p1p3pp/2Np1n2/2b5/4P3/2N5/PPP2P.text: Qe8 gives us good compensation, as we attack the knight, plus we have additional pressure on e4 (which we'll win) and we'll have pressure on f2 as well.

r1b1qrk1/p1p3pp/2pp1n2/8/3bP3/2NN4/PPP2P.text: We apply pressure on e4. We have open lines and the bishop pair - good compensation for the pawn.

r1b1qrk1/p1pp2pp/2p2n2/4N3/4P3/2P5/P1P2P.text: Attack the knight and x-ray e4 behind it, ensuring we'll regain our pawn.

r1bq1r1k/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1BbNp1B1/4P3/5N2/.text:
We get our king off of the dangerous diagonal.

To be clear: we are not afraid of Nxf6 gxf6. We'd like the g-file to open up for our rook! 

The d4-square, if available, would also be a good square for our c6-knight.

r1bq1rk1/p1p3pp/2pp1n2/2b5/4P3/2NN4/PPP2.text:
White goes back to d3 where it attacks our bishop.

We move away from danger, putting pressure on the white center.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp2pp/2p2n2/2b1N3/4P3/2N5/PPP.text:
White develops, protecting e4.

Development is key. We will play to open up our light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp2pp/2p2n2/4N3/4P3/2P5/P1P2P.text: If the knight takes, we can...

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p1B1/4P3/2P2N2.text:
Now we can start placing our pawns on dark squares, given that we've traded our dark-squared bishop. We have the superior pawn structure.

We want to play ...Qe8, ...Be6, and safety moves like ...Kh8. 

If Bc4 at some point, we don't mind a trade of bishops and to maneuver the knight with ...Nd8. 

Our queen from e8 can then go to the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/pppp2pp/2B2n2/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/P1P.text:
White can also take, removing the defender of e5.

We'll capture towards the center.

r1bqk2r/p1pp2pp/2p2n2/2b1N3/4P3/8/PPP2PP.text:
White grabs a pawn! Oh no! They can do this?

We'll just castle, and prioritize our development. We are going to play gambit style.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B1Np1B1/4P3/5N2/P.text:
White captures.

And we can capture on e4 with check, unpinning and attacking the g5-bishop!

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1Bb1p1B1/4P3/2N2N2.text:
White pins us.

But we can now castle when our rook supports the knight on f6.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1BbNp1B1/4P3/5N2/P.text:
Nd5 applies pressure on our pinned piece.

But here we have a tactical trick, taking on f2 with check!

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np4/1B1Np1B1/4n3/5N2/PPP.text:
The king retreats.

We'll take the bishop that was attacking us.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2np4/1B1Np1N1/8/8/PPP3PP/.text:
White recaptures.

And we'll recapture, too. We're now two pawns up, but c7 is loose.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2B2n2/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Bxc6 damaging our structure is a valid continuation.

Your opponents will remove the defender of the e5-pawn here 24% of the time.

We'll capture towards the center.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/1b2P3/2N2N2/.text:
White unpins by castling.

But we'll capture, damaging the white pawn structure.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/2P2N2/P1.text:
White recaptures.

And we get castled ourselves.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1Bb1p1B1/4P3/2N2N2.text:
White develops to c3.

Now that our bishop is outside of the pawns we'll play d6.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1Bb1p3/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
White can choose to develop a piece defending e4. This is the most common move, played 30% of the time. 

We'll reply with ...d6. It's worth noting that White will occasionally play Qd3 here instead of Nc3. Here, too, we should play d6, and protect our bishop against any sneaky forks with Qc4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p1B1/4P3/5N2/P.text:
Bg5 pins the attacker of e4.

Expect to see it 12% of the time.

We can temporarily ignore the pin and develop our bishop aiming at f2.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
Nc3 defends the pawn on e4.

It's the most popular and natural-looking move, played 36% of the time.

We can pin the knight with Bb4!

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
White here can castle, as we're not prepared to take on e4 because of our lack of development.

And they will 28% of the time.

We can now develop our bishop outside of the pawn chain before we play d6.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
And White plays the Ruy Lopez, attacking the defender of e5.

With ...f5, we offer up a pawn! This is our gambit! White has many plausible responses. In this study we'll analyze 4.d3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
White recaptures.

Now we can develop and attack e4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/3P1N2/PP.text:
White chooses to defend e4 with another pawn. Very logical, and the kind of move an unprepared opponent could well find.

This move is played 26% of the time, which is around 450,000 games.

We'll capture on e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn with Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Jaenisch Gambit! 

This chapter will deal with the main lines within this gambit. Hence why the positions we'll analyze in this study happen after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5, and then the very logical 4.d3. 

White opens with the king's pawn. We'll reply with ...e5.

2kr1bnr/pppb2pp/2p5/5p2/8/3P1N2/PPP1KPPP.text: And we castle long, with an active position.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/5p2/3qP3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
White returns the knight, attacking our queen.

And now we regain the pawn. We have acquired the bishop pair.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/5p2/4q3/5N2/PPPPQPPP.text:
Play can continue with White blocking, offering a queen trade.

We'll develop the bishop with Bd7. We are happy for White to exchange queens and bring our pawn to a dominant square.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2p2n2/4p3/4N3/5N2/PPPPQP.text:
White recaptures.

We'll develop our light-squared bishop and pin the f3-knight.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2p2n2/4pp2/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White defends e4.

Let's just trade that central pawn.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
White takes the undefended pawn. This happens in 48% of games.

This is the main point behind Bxc6.

We'll fork the knight and pawn!

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/4pp2/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
White defends e4 with a knight.

This "less tactical" approach is chosen 5% of the time.

We'll apply pressure to e4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
And White plays the Ruy Lopez, attacking the defender of e5.

With ...f5, the Jaenisch Gambit, we offer up a pawn! In this study we'll analyze 4.Bxc6.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2B5/4pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
White eliminates our knight, removing a supporter of our center.

This is the most popular move and it's played in almost 500,000 games, which is 28%.

We'll take away from the center, opening up our bishop and queen.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2p2n2/4p3/4N1b1/5N1P/PPPP.text:
White challenges our bishop.

We'll capture the knight.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/2p2n2/4p3/4N3/5Q1P/PPPP1P.text:
The queen recaptures.

We'll trade on e4.

r3kb1r/ppp3pp/2p5/3qp3/4Q3/7P/PPPP1PP1/R.text: And we propose yet another trade. The position is equal.

r3kbnr/pppb2pp/2p5/5p2/4q3/3P1N2/PPP1QPP.text:
White presses for the exchange of queens, but not on e4.

We'll take on e2.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn with Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Since the Jaenisch arises out of the Ruy Lopez, we must ask the question: what if White chooses to take our knight on c6 with the bishop? 

This study aims to answer that question by giving you some dynamic options against this as well.

White opens with the king's pawn.
We'll reply with ...e5.

r1b1kb1r/p1pp2pp/2p2n2/4qP2/4p3/5N2/PPPP.text:
White takes advantage of the pin!

But they do not stop us from capturing the pawn on f5.

r1b1kb1r/p1pp2pp/2p2n2/5q2/4p3/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
The rook comes to the e-file.

Now with Kf7, we get out of the pin and threaten the knight on f3.

r1b1kb1r/p1ppq1pp/2p2n2/5P2/3Np3/8/PPPPQ.text:
After castling, we need to bear in mind that White will bring the rook to e1.

We'll attack the defender of f5 by playing Qe5.

r1b1kbnr/p1ppq1pp/2p5/5P2/3Np3/8/PPPPQPP.text:
The white knight comes forward, trying to defend the pawn they grabbed on f5.

We need to address the possibility of Qh5+, so we'll develop our knight and defend e4 in the process. Our control of the center is greater than White's.

r1b1kbnr/ppppq1pp/2B5/5P2/4p3/5N2/PPPPQP.text:
White removes our knight from c6. This was the idea of 3. Bb5, so they might as well follow through.

Let's recapture towards the center. The f3-knight remains en prise!

r1b1r3/p1pp1kpp/2pb1n2/4q3/4p2N/3P2P1/PP.text:
And now our queen is sufficiently defended and our defence of e4 is great! 

A good plan for the near future would be to get the bishop to c5 since White has played g3, and then play for ...d5.

If White attacks our queen with Bf4, we can retreat it to e7.

r1b2b1r/p1pp1kpp/2p2n2/4q3/4p2N/3P4/PPP1.text:
White can try the very natural d3, seeing that our e-pawn is pinned.

We'll develop our bishop, setting up a battery attacking h2!

r1b2b1r/p1pp1kpp/2p2n2/5q2/4p2N/8/PPPPQP.text:
The knight can gain a tempo on us.

But we can move back to e5, with an eye on h2.

r1b4r/p1pp1kpp/2pb1n2/4q3/4p2N/3P2P1/PPP.text: After g3, our rook can enter the game.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/5P2/4p3/5N2/PPPPQPPP.text:
White pins the e-pawn.

We'll take on f5 and defend e4 with our bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
And White plays the Ruy Lopez, attacking the defender of e5.

With ...f5, we offer up a pawn! This is our gambit! White has many plausible responses. In this study we'll analyze what happens if White captures on f5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2B5/5P2/4p3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
White has a piece under attack. They thus choose to exchange! But this is the wrong approach.

And you'll face this wrong approach 46% of the time!

We'll capture away from the center, opening up our queen and light-squared bishop. This latter piece in particular attacks f5!

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pP2/8/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
If White chooses to take, they play into our hand! 

And they will do so 25% of the time, which is about 440,000 games.

Now with ...e4 we will control the center and bully them!

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B3P2/4p3/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
The queen intervenes, attacking our pawn and pinning it to our king! 

Expect to see this move a third of the time, 33%.

We'll break the pin and defend e4 by playing Qe7.

r2qkbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/5b2/4p3/3P1N2/PPP1QPP.text: With d3, White increases pressure on the pinned pawn.

r3kbnr/ppp1q1pp/2p5/5b2/4p3/3P1N2/PPP1QP.text: Thus we defend it once more, breaking the pin. It seems we offered a gambit in the opening, but we're still equal, and we have the bishop pair!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn with Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Let's delve deep into the final study of the chapter.

White can choose to continue by just taking the pawn offered to them.

In this case, we have everything we want! The central control is ours. After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.exf5, we'll have 4...e4 attacking the knight, and a fun game for sure! 

Let's start with 1.e4 and our reply of ...e5!

1r3rk1/p1p3pp/2pp1b2/8/6b1/3PBN2/PPP2PPP.text:
Our rook enters the semi-open file where it threatens b2.

In the future, we might capture White's knight on f3 and double their pawns.

Moves like ...d5 and ...Re8 come to mind, as well.

r1b1k2r/p1p1b1pp/2pp1Q2/8/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White accepts the trade.

We'll recapture, bringing our bishop to an active post on f6.

r1b1k2r/p1p1b1pp/2pp2q1/4P3/8/5N2/PPP1QP.text:
White takes the coveted e5 pawn.

But we'll play actively and castle, with ideas of Bh3 or Bg4.

r1b1k2r/p1p3pp/2pp1b2/8/8/3P1N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White opens up their bishop.

We'll simply castle into safety.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p1q3/8/8/5N2/PPPPQPPP/.text:
The knight retreats. White couldn't simply castle because of d6.

We'll exchange queens and leave the white king in the center.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p2q2/4N3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/.text:
White wins the e5 pawn, but we have the bishop pair.

We'll switch our queen to the e-file, pinning the knight and posing some questions.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p2q2/4Q3/8/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
White grabs the pawn in the center.

Let's go for quick development with d6.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p2q2/4p3/3P4/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
Another possibility is d4, when White adds yet another attacker on e5.

Here we should sidestep and attack g2.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p3q1/4p3/3P4/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
White castles, defending g2.

We'll play d6 and open up our light-squared bishop.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/2p5/8/8/5N2/PPPPKPPP/R1.text:
White recaptures.

After ...c5, our bishop is coming out where it'll control the diagonals unopposed.

r1b1k2r/p1ppb1pp/8/2p5/8/5N2/PPPPKPPP/R1.text:
The rook steps into the open file.

We'll place our bishop actively on b7.

r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2B2q2/4p3/8/5N2/PPPPQPP.text:
White takes the defender of e5.

We'll capture towards the center.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
White applies pressure to e5.

Let's prepare castling by playing Be7. White can win a pawn, but if they do so we will have compensation.

r1b1qbk1/p6p/2p1rp2/2pp4/Q7/4BN2/PPP2PPP.text: And we double major pieces on the e-file while adding another defender on c6.

r1b2rk1/p1p3pp/2pp1b2/8/8/3P1N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
White has to waste a move like this, because otherwise their bishop was tied to the b-pawn.

We'll give ourselves the option of doubling White's pawns.

r1b2rk1/ppp3bp/2n2q2/1B1p4/8/5N2/PPP1QPP.text: We can here just recapture and we're up in development, with open lines for our bishops and heavy pieces.

r1bq1bk1/p1p4p/4rp2/1Qpp4/8/4BN2/PPP2PPP.text:
The rook puts pressure on our center but most importantly, removes itself from skewer territory!

We'll attack the queen and support our center with ...c6.

r1bq1bk1/p6p/2p1rp2/2pp4/Q7/4BN2/PPP2PPP.text: The queen drops back one square.

r1bq1rk1/p1p3bp/2p1Pp2/3p4/8/5N2/PPP1QPP.text:
White pushes their e-pawn so that when we recapture our pawns remain split.

We'll play Re8, preparing to recover the pawn.

r1bq1rk1/pp4bp/2p1Pp2/3pn3/5B2/3B1N2/PPP.text:
White retreats.

We'll take the bishop pair!

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2B2p2/3pP3/8/5N2/PPP1QPP.text:
White removes the piece that covered the e5 square.

We'll recapture.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2n1Pp2/1B1p4/8/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
White doesn't give up the pawn so easily.

We'll bring our knight into the center.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/4Pp2/1B1pn3/5B2/5N2/PPP1.text:
White develops putting pressure on our knight.

We'll attack the bishop with ...c6 and cement our structure.

r1bqk2r/ppp3bp/2n2p2/1B1pP3/8/5N2/PPP1QP.text:
White can actually take it.

But we'll castle and play for activity.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2N2/1B1pp3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
White captures on f6.

We'll recapture with the pawn and build a strong center.

r1bqkb1r/ppp4p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/3P4/5N2/PPP1.text:
Attacking the pinned pawn.

We'll support the structure and prepare to castle.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2N2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White agrees 37% of the time.

We'll recapture with the queen.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPP.text:
White can choose to defend e4 with the queen.

They do so 18% of the time.

We'll push in the center with ...d5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
And White plays the Ruy Lopez, attacking the defender of e5.

With ...f5, we enter our gambit! White has many plausible responses. In this study we'll analyze how to respond when White plays 4.Nc3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll develop our king's knight and propose a trade.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White defends e4 with the knight.

This is the fourth most popular move, played 11% of the time, which is almost 200,000 games.

We'll capture on e4.

r1bqr1k1/p1p3bp/2p1Pp2/3p4/8/5N2/PPP1QPP.text:
White castles.

We'll play c5, taking d4 away from the knight.

r1bqr1k1/p1p3bp/4Pp2/1Qpp4/8/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
The queen heads to b5 to pressure our pawns from the side.

Our bishop can defend from f8.

r1bqrbk1/p1p4p/4Pp2/1Qpp4/8/4BN2/PPP2PPP.text:
White increases pressure.

But here we can take the pawn already with the rook, threatening Ba6, with a skewer!

r2q1rk1/pp4bp/2p1bp2/3p4/5B2/3Q1N2/PPP2P.text: And now we can recapture with our bishop on e6, with ideas of repositioning it to g6.

r3k2r/pbppb1pp/8/2p5/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R1B1.text: We are now pinned on the e-file, but we can damage White's pawn structure...

r3kr2/p1ppb1pp/8/2p5/8/5P2/PPPP1P1P/R1B1.text: We enter the f-file and begin pressuring f3.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn with Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of the sidelines chapter! 

We'll study positions after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.Nc3. Defending the e-pawn with the knight is actually considered a mainline, so let's pay extra attention and make sure to learn the moves!

White opens with the king's pawn. We'll reply with ...e5.

5r2/pp3k1p/3Pbnp1/1p6/8/8/PPP2PPP/R4RK1.text: And we recapture, with a favorable ending. We have two pieces for the rook. Our rook will come to d8 and our knight to d5. We'll be winning the advanced d-pawn shortly.

N4b1r/pp1k3p/3Pbp2/4q3/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R2Q.text:
This check is very compelling. White loses castling rights.

Their rook on h1 will have a hard time developing.

Furthermore, a simple ...Bxd6 will open up an attack on the knight and White cannot save it.

N4b1r/pp1k3p/3Pbp2/q7/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R2QK.text: What if White just grabs the rook?

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/3P1B2/q7/1p6/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
White saves a piece by taking one.

We'll recapture on f6.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/3P1n2/qp4B1/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
The knight blocks.

We'll push ...b4 and attack two pieces.

r1b1kb1r/pp5p/3P1p2/q2N4/1p6/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The white knight leaps forward, threatening to come to c7.

...b3+ is our best move here.

r1b1kb1r/pp5p/3P1p2/q2N4/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R.text:
c3 blocks.

And now we go for maximum development!

r1b1kbnr/pp1p2pp/2p5/q3P3/2B1p3/8/PPP2PP.text: This check is a fork! We'll take on e5 and play d5, with an extra pawn and a strong center.

r1b1qb1r/pp3kpp/3P4/1p2B3/4Q3/8/PPP2PPP/.text: The bishop interposes, blocking the pin and the trade proposal.

r1b1qb1r/pp4pp/3P2k1/1p1QB3/8/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White blocks it.

We'll propose a trade of queens!

r1b1qrk1/ppp3pp/2pb1n2/4N1B1/3Pp3/2N5/PP.text:
We can get out of the pin and pressure e5.

Next, developing moves like ...Bf5 and ...Qg6 are great if the knight moves, to get some pieces to the kingside.

Centralizing the a-rook is always a good idea.

r1b2b1r/pp3kpp/2qP4/1p2B3/4Q3/8/PPP2PPP/.text: Trade! Once more! After any check, we'll be safe on g8. Just don't undefend the light squares!

r1b2b1r/pp4pp/2qP2k1/1p2B3/3Q4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
White obviously rejects it.

But we'll keep trying to trade!

r1bq1b1Q/pp3k1p/3P1npB/1p6/8/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White applies pressure on our pinned bishop, not least because their queen has no squares.

But now we can just develop to e6 and our queen is defended by the rook.

r1bq1b1Q/pp3k1p/3P2p1/1p6/4n3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White is advised to take the most valuable piece. Our h-pawn is under attack.

Thus we fall back with Nf6 and defend the pawn.

r1bq1b1r/pp3kpp/3P4/1p1Q4/8/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
White may continue trying to harass us.

The king can safely come upwards. White doesn't have enough active pieces to mount a dangerous attack.

r1bq1b1r/pp3kpp/3P4/1p6/4QB2/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Again, White may recognize one attacker isn't enough, so a second one is brought in. (But it's not fast enough, and the bishop doesn't coordinate well with the queen).

We propose a queen trade, as we pin the queen to the king, and we place ourselves on a light square to defend that color complex.

r1bq1b1r/pp4pp/3P2k1/1p1Q4/5B2/8/PPP2PPP.text:
The other attacker joins a little too late.

We'll check with our queen.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2pb1n2/4N1B1/3Pp3/2N5/PP.text: Another piece adds pressure to e4.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2pb1n2/4N1B1/3Pp3/2N5/PPP.text:
The bishop pins our knight.

We'll get our king to safety and support our knight with the rook.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/3P1n2/1p4B1/4N3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Another idea is for White to pin our knight, attacking it with two pieces.

We'll give a check and unpin with tempo!

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/3P1n2/1p6/3QN3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
The queen is brought to pressurize f6, though this isn't the best move.

Let's remove one of the attackers!

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/3P1n2/1p6/4N3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White castles, with the idea of bringing a rook into the attack.

We'll take on e4, but our king is very open and we'll need to be precise in our play.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/3P4/1p5Q/4n3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
Check!

Here we block with the pawn. We're ultimately losing the rook on h8, but the alternative is ...Kd7 Qxb5+ and our king gets drawn into the center of the board.

r1bqkb1r/pp4pp/3P4/1p6/4Q3/8/PPP2PPP/R1B.text:
White recaptures, giving check.

Luckily our king can come out and be perfectly fine. He'll be safe on the light squares! Notice there's only one attacker at the moment, the queen. This is less dangerous than being attacked by many pieces!

r1bqkb1r/pp5p/3P2p1/1p2Q3/4n3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Check! Forking our pieces.

Let's bring the king up, away from the e-file and into a safer position.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2p2n2/4N3/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Nc3 applies pressure on e4.

We'll develop to d6, pressurizing the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p2pp/2p5/1B2P3/4p3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Craziness on the board! The bishop is hanging! But White argues they have counterplay.

Only 14% of players will know about this tricky move.

We'll take the bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p2pp/2p5/4P3/2B1p3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
This simple retreats lets us have what we want.

And it's played 61% of the time!

r1bqkbnr/pp1p2pp/8/1p2P3/4N3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White captures our pawn in the center. Careful! There are some lines open to our king!

With ...d5, we give up a pawn but facilitate our development.

r1bqkbnr/pp4pp/3P4/1p6/4N3/8/PPP2PPP/R1B.text:
En passant! White is obviously a cultured individual.

We see an immediate benefit of giving up our d-pawn, and can now develop the knight to f6.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2p5/4N3/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
The knight gets out of danger.

We'll develop, supporting e4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
The Ruy Lopez, threatening the stability of our center!

With ...f5, we enter our gambit!

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2B5/4p3/3Pp3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Alternatively, White can diminish our central defense by taking off the knight. 

This is played 22% of the time.

Capturing away from the center unleashes both queen and light-squared bishop!

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2N3/3Pp3/8/PPP2PP.text:
White captures one of our pawns and gets out of danger.

Expect to see this move by far the most, 74% of the time.

Let's take on e5! White would've been willing to take us on c6 either way. Now the bishop on b5 is misplaced, surely.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/3PP3/5N2/PPP.text:
White counters in the center! Notice each pawn in the center can be captured! 

This tricky move is played 5% of the time, which is around 80,000 games.

Best is to capture on e4, destabilizing the knight on f3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/1B2P3/4p3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Recapturing.

By playing c6, we gain a tempo on the bishop! Additionally, we open up the diagonal so our queen can check on a5, followed by taking on e5!

r2q1B1Q/pp3k1p/3Pbnp1/1p6/8/8/PPP2PPP/R4.text:
Thus trading is the best they can do.

And we'll recapture.

r3kb1r/ppN4p/3Pbp2/q7/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R2QK.text:
White checks us.

We'll protect the e6-bishop, and hide behind the d-pawn.

r4b1r/pp4pp/3P2k1/1p2Bb2/2q5/4Q3/PPP2PPP.text: And we develop another piece! We might propose a trade that cannot be denied next move.

r4b1r/ppNk3p/3Pbp2/q7/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R2Q1.text:
White can castle in hopes of bringing another attacker.

We'll take the knight's defender, forcing the issue.

r6r/pp1k3p/3bNp2/4q3/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R2QR1.text:
We're basically allowing white to try to preserve their material because of the counterplay we're getting.

We'll take on h2 with check.

r6r/pp1k3p/3bNp2/8/8/1pP5/PP2KPP1/R2QR2q.text: White moves out of the way.

r6r/pp1k3p/3bNp2/8/8/1pP5/PP2KPq1/R2QR3.text:
We grab on g2. As you can see, the knight is still alive on e6, but White's king is doing terribly! 

Besides, our rooks will be coming to the e- and d-files. 

The rook coming to the d-file must be timed though, as there's a knight controlling that square.

r6r/pp1k3p/3bNp2/8/8/1pP5/PP3PPq/R2QRK2.text:
White steps away.

We'll give another check to force the king out and then we will take on g2.

r6r/pp1k3p/3bNp2/q7/8/1pP5/PP3PPP/R2Q1RK.text:
This capture is better as it draws our king out and takes away one of our good defenders.

But we're not obligated to recapture! Instead, we can threaten mate on h2!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn with Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this study we'll go over the position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5 4.d4! You can mentally refer to this position as White counterattacks in the center.

Let's begin! 

White opens with the king's pawn. We'll reply with ...e5.

r1bq1rk1/ppppb1pp/2n2n2/1B2N3/3Pp3/2P5/P.text:
And here we can castle safely, with ideas of d7-d5 consolidating our pawn on e4, after the pressure on c6 is resolved.

If the knights are traded, we can get a piece to the g4-square.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2nb1n2/1B2p3/3P4/5N2/PPP.text:
White pushes, attacking our center, and trying to exploit the pin on the e-file.

We'll push the e-pawn and eye the f3-knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2nb1n2/1B6/3Pp3/2P2N2/PP.text:
White consolidates d4.

But now we can unpin our e-pawn by repositioning our bishop to e7!

r1bqk2r/ppppb1pp/2n2n2/1B2N3/3Pp3/2P5/PP.text: White's knight was under attack so they decide to jump into a central location.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
The queen goes back.

We'll develop, supporting e5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
The Ruy Lopez, threatening the stability of our center!

With ...f5, we enter our gambit!

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4Q3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White recaptures with the queen as originally intended.

We can develop with a tempo on the queen.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
White defends e4 with the queen. 

This move is only played 1% of the time, in around 12,000 games, but that doesn't mean you won't come across it!

At this juncture, I suggest capturing.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
The knight attacks e5.

We'll defend the pawn with Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This study is pretty straightforward. We reach our standard gambit opening with 1.e4 e5 2. f3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5, and white defends e4 with 4.Qe2.

You'll achieve equality pretty quickly in this line, so there's no need to worry!

Let's begin! White opens with the king's pawn. We'll reply with ...e5.
